title: Is It Okay for Parents to Use AI to Advocate for Their Kids?
author: Bette Ludwig
summary: Drawing on nearly 20 years in higher education, 15 of them as an academic advisor, Bette Ludwig challenges the binary, all-good-or-all-bad framing many parents apply to AI in education by pointing to concrete cases where AI is helping families navigate systems that were previously opaque or gatekept. She cites a 29.6% year-over-year increase in Connecticut special-education complaint filings, which experts partly attribute to parents using tools like ChatGPT to understand special-education law and draft formal advocacy paperwork, and contrasts this with her own cousin's pre-AI, decade-long self-taught fight to secure services for a son with cerebral palsy. She extends the argument to financial aid, arguing that AI is exposing higher education's reliance on unwritten rules and vague requirements, forcing financial-aid offices to redesign appeals processes as more families use AI to understand what's actually required. The piece closes by citing a survey finding more than half of parents now use AI to help evaluate colleges (researching internships, job placement, and career prospects), and argues that the 'ship' of hoping parents and students would simply stop using AI has already sailed.
points: Cites a concrete, sourced statistic — a 29.6% increase in Connecticut special-education complaint filings from 2023-24 to 2024-25 — that experts partly attribute to parents using AI to understand special-education law and draft advocacy paperwork.

Frames AI-assisted parent advocacy as a power shift that institutions (schools, districts, state education agencies, financial aid offices) need to prepare for rather than resist, since 'the AI ship of hoping students and parents stop using it has sailed.'

Uses a personal, pre-AI family story (a cousin who spent years self-teaching special-education law and advocacy to support a son with cerebral palsy) to illustrate what parents can now do faster and with more confidence using AI tools.

Challenges the false equivalence between 'using AI' and 'not wanting to think,' arguing instead that AI can help parents understand systems (special education law, financial aid appeals) they might never have understood on their own.

Notes that more than half of surveyed parents now use AI to evaluate colleges for their kids (researching internships, job placement rates, career prospects, and earning potential), suggesting AI-assisted college search has already become mainstream rather than fringe behavior.
quotes: So many parents still see AI, or ChatGPT more specifically, as a tool students use to cheat, or they have conscientious objections to it. There's this very binary thinking surrounding it. It's either all good or all bad, with nothing in between.

Connecticut saw a 29.6% increase in special education complaint filings from 2023-24 to 2024-25. Experts say increased understanding of special education law may be contributing to the increase, and some specifically point to parents' use of AI.
Think about what parents can do now when they have a resource that can help them with that: how to understand the laws, figure out what questions to ask, and help them actually write the letters.

Financial aid offices are now complaining that the growing number of appeals is creating an incredible workflow problem because more students and parents are submitting them with the help of tools like ChatGPT.
I think it's pretty safe to say that the AI ship of hoping students and parents stop using it has sailed so far over the horizon you can't even see it anymore.
According to a recent survey, more than 50% of parents are now using AI to help them decide which colleges to send their kids to.
